cases.note: The bytes that cross when everything is right. Rates are per second and over the monotonic duration, and the five counters nothing measured are named rather than reported as zero.

A robot with no kernel running: five minutes of being up, and nothing counted. It is a valid window — "the robot was up for five minutes and counted nothing" is a fact — and it is what every robot this edition runs will send.
The distinction §74.3 exists for, beside the case above. Zero guard trips and no measurement of guard trips render identically as 0, and the second is the number an operator relaxes on.
Nothing to divide by, so no rate is anything. Refused rather than counted as zero — a rate of zero over no time is the most confident wrong number a fleet page can render.

cases.note: Exactly 60,000 ms of disagreement, which is **not** implausible: the test is strictly greater, and every skew in this corpus was either zero or an hour. A robot whose clock is corrected by exactly a minute is at the value an operator will read as the threshold, so this is the case that says which side of it the threshold falls on.

And the same value the other way, because the test is two comparisons rather than one over an absolute value. An edition writing `Math.abs(skew) >= 60_000` agrees with this one everywhere except on the two boundaries themselves.

A negative count is not a count. It is a counter that wrapped, or a field somebody defaulted to −1, and it lands in `unmeasured` rather than producing a negative rate on a fleet page — which is a number nobody can read and which would drag a total below the counts that are real. The `< 0` arm of the three-way test had no case.

The other side of the same guard. `elapsed_ms: 0` is refused by a case above; a **negative** duration was not, and the two are different code paths once a report has to decide what to put in `elapsed_ms`. It is zero, because a window that reports a negative duration has reported no duration — passing it through would put a negative denominator into `observed_ms`.
